d.title: Two metrics, four verdicts, and no theorising required
d.caption: This is the cheapest diagnostic in the module: **context recall and faithfulness read together name the broken layer.** Low recall with high faithfulness is a **retrieval** failure — the model was scrupulously faithful to context that did not contain the answer. High recall with low faithfulness is a **generation** failure. High on both means neither moved and the **ground truth or the judge** did, which is the case people never consider. Low on both is systemic: an empty index, the wrong tenant, a truncated prompt.

cells.text: the ground truth or the judge moved

d.title: The incident, metric by metric
d.caption: Answer accuracy fell from 0.95 to 0.60 — the symptom. **Context recall collapsed from 0.93 to 0.48 and faithfulness did not move at all**, staying at 0.95, which is exactly §01's retrieval-failure signature. The mechanism is two rows lower: mean top-1 similarity went from 0.78 to 0.41. And the last row is the one that would have caught it weeks earlier: **empty-retrieval rate from 0.4% to 11.2%, an alarm nobody had set**, costing nothing to compute.

d.title: Slice before you theorise: a 21% cohort inside a 60% headline
d.caption: The headline fell from 0.95 to 0.60 and the average is a **mix of two populations behaving completely differently.** Questions about existing docs are 60% of traffic and fell from 0.96 to 0.86 — unwelcome and unremarkable. Questions about the new product line are 40% of traffic and fell from 0.86 to **0.21**. One slice turns "quality regressed" into "the new product line has no usable documents in the index", which is a different investigation and a different fix.

d.title: Walking the stack bottom-up, attribute by attribute
d.caption: Comparing a healthy trace against a failing one, **most attributes are identical** — same index, same 20 results returned, same pinned model, no truncation. Three differ and they tell the whole story: **`above_threshold` is 0 against 6**, so nothing cleared the cut-off; `rerank.top_score` is **0.31 against 0.78**, so the best available chunk was weakly related; and the chunk IDs are all from the **old** product manual. The search worked perfectly and there was nothing right to find.

d.title: Two experiments, ten minutes, no metrics and no labels
d.caption: Before any statistics: **run the retriever on its own with no model involved.** Give it the failing queries and look at what comes back — if the right chunk is not there, you have a retrieval problem and nothing about the model matters. **Then run the generator with hand-picked perfect context**: paste in the chunks that should have been retrieved, and if the answer is now correct, generation is fine. Between them they name the broken layer with **no metrics, no judge and no labels** — the statistical version needs a labelled set and a day.

d.title: Slice freely in an incident, sparingly in an alert rule
d.caption: The runbook says to slice, and it is right — 10.13 found a 21% cohort inside a 60% headline. But **every slice divides the sample**, and 10.12's arithmetic says the detectable effect grows as the slice shrinks. Neither the runbook nor the alerting guidance mentions this, and **the two instructions genuinely conflict**. The resolution is to separate the activities: slicing is for investigation, where you already know something is wrong and are hunting for where. For small slices you do want to alert on, lengthen the window instead.

d.title: Eight pitfalls, and the step each one breaks
d.caption: The first is the one that makes everything else impossible: **retrieval and generation failures look identical in the final answer, so you cannot debug what you did not capture.** The third is the one that makes "nothing changed" unprovable — model alias, embedding model, prompt template, index and chunking config, and without **all five** the claim cannot be checked. And the seventh is 10.10's finding: head sampling at 5% keeps a random 5% and throws away the failures.
